BUCSS

BUCSS is an R package for implementing Bias and Uncertainty Corrected Sample Size planning. BUCSS implements a method of correcting for publication bias and uncertainty when planning the sample size of a future study from an original study. See Anderson, Kelley, & Maxwell (2017; Psychological Science, 28, 1547–1562).

Installing BUCSS

Install the released version from CRAN:

install.packages("BUCSS")

Then load the package:

library(BUCSS)

The ss_buc_* function family described below is the current BUCSS interface, introduced in 2.0.0. The development version lives on GitHub:

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("yelleKneK/BUCSS")

Using BUCSS

Consider an original study in which two independent groups are used to test the null hypothesis of no difference in the population means of the two groups (e.g., a treatment and a control group). Suppose the independent samples t test in the original study reported t = 3.00, with 50 and 55 participants in the two groups and a Type I error rate of .05. The planned study seeks a statistical power of .80 with 90% assurance that the power will be at least .80.

result <- ss_buc_independent_t(t_observed = 3, n = c(50, 55), alpha_prior = .05,
                               alpha_planned = .05, desired_power = .80,
                               assurance = .90)
result
#>  term                  value
#>  necessary_n_per_group 1485
#>  total_N               2970
#>  actual_power          0.803
#>  ncp_adjusted          0.526
#>  smd_planning          0.103
#>  t_observed            3
#>  n_1                   50
#>  n_2                   55
#>  alpha_prior           0.05
#>  alpha_planned         0.05
#>  assurance             0.9
#>  desired_power         0.8
#>
#> Design: Independent t test
#> Sample size unit: per group
#> Largest supportable assurance: .93

This yields a necessary sample size of 1,485 per group (a total of 2,970). BUCSS 1.x reported 1,482 for this example under its grid search; as of BUCSS 2.0.0 the bias and uncertainty adjusted noncentrality parameter is found by direct root finding, which gives 1,485 (see NEWS.md). The row smd_planning is the planning effect size, an adjusted effect size: the value, in the design’s usual effect size metric, used to plan the sample size given the situation at hand (the prior study’s result, the publication bias assumed through alpha_prior, and the uncertainty allowed for through assurance). Here it is the adjusted noncentrality parameter restated as a standardized mean difference, 0.103, where the prior study’s t taken at face value corresponds to 0.586. It is what the plan is built on, not an estimate of the effect to report. A study of 1,485 per group has exactly the actual_power shown when the population standardized mean difference equals the planning effect size.

Assurance is the long run proportion of studies planned this way, each from its own published prior study, whose power at the true effect reaches the desired power. BUCSS delivers it by planning from the lower limit of a one-sided confidence interval for the prior study’s noncentrality parameter, at a confidence level equal to the assurance, computed from the distribution of the prior statistic truncated at the publication threshold. An assurance of .5 plans from the median unbiased estimate and corrects for publication bias only; above .5 it also corrects for uncertainty. The term follows Kelley and Maxwell (2003), who used assurance in sample size planning for the probability that a confidence interval will be no wider than desired.

The publication threshold is alpha_prior: the significance level a prior result had to reach to be published (more generally, to reach you). The correction assumes you see only results with p below alpha_prior, .05 by default. Setting alpha_prior = 1, which may also be written alpha_prior = "No Publication Filter", means no publication filter: every p value is at most 1, so any result would have been published whatever its p value, there is no publication bias to correct, and only the correction for uncertainty, set by assurance, remains, as for a pilot study. Anderson, Kelley, and Maxwell (2017, p. 1552) note that the level can be set equal to 1 when publication bias is thought not to apply.

For this prior study, the plan grows with the assurance requested: 60 per group at an assurance of .50, 233 at .80, and 1,485 at .90. Taking t = 3.00 at face value would plan 47 per group. The prior result supports an assurance of at most about .93 (the “Largest supportable assurance” the printed result reports), and the plan grows without bound as that ceiling approaches, which plot() draws. vignette("understanding-assurance", package = "BUCSS") explains both settings.

The functions return a tidy object of class bucss_plan, shaped like the result tables in the DMAR package: an ordinary data.frame of term/value rows holding the design results (the size row is named for its unit, here necessary_n_per_group, and the planning effect size row for its metric, here smd_planning) followed by rows echoing the planning inputs, so the assumptions travel with the result:

result$value[result$term == "necessary_n_per_group"]  # 1485
result$value[result$term == "actual_power"]           # power at that size
result$value[result$term == "ncp_adjusted"]           # adjusted noncentrality
result$value[result$term == "smd_planning"]           # planning effect size, 0.103

The broom verbs give the two convenient views. tidy() is the compact estimate view (term, estimate, power), as in DMAR’s sample size planners, and glance() the one-row wide view, which begins with those same three columns, as DMAR’s does, and then, unlike DMAR’s, keeps every row of the result as a column (so the sample size and actual_power appear twice):

tidy(result)               # term = "sample_size", estimate = 1485, power
tidy(result)$estimate      # 1485
glance(result)             # term, estimate, power, then every row as a column
planning_sentence(result)  # the sentences for a manuscript

What’s New Since 1.2.1

BUCSS 2.0.0 is the first release since 1.2.1. NEWS.md has the full list; the main changes follow.

A New Interface

The functions are renamed to the ss_buc_* prefix (for example ss_buc_independent_t() in place of ss.power.it()), so the names make clear that these planners apply the bias and uncertainty correction rather than ordinary power analysis. Arguments are snake_case, and the 1.x power is now desired_power. Each function returns the tidy bucss_plan object shown above rather than a two-element list, with print(), tidy(), and glance() methods, a knitr method that renders the same table in R Markdown, and planning_sentence(), which writes the planning sentences for a manuscript. The independent and paired t test planners also carry effect size aliases (ss_buc_smd() and ss_buc_smd_paired()), and the between-subjects ANOVA is split into a one-way planner (ss_buc_one_way_anova()) and a two-way planner (ss_buc_factorial_anova()).

The old dotted names still run but are deprecated: each forwards to its ss_buc_* replacement and issues a one-time-per-session warning naming the new function. The object it returns keeps the 1.x positional extraction working, so legacy code that reads result[[1]] (the necessary sample size) and result[[2]] (the adjusted noncentrality parameter) continues to work. Only those two literal subscripts are kept: code that treats the result as a plain two-element list in other ways, such as unlist(result) or an integer subscript like result[[1L]], sees the new data frame instead.

Eighteen Designs

Six designs join the twelve that 1.2.1 covered:

Design Function
One-sample, paired, independent, and Welch t tests ss_buc_one_sample_t(), ss_buc_paired_t(), ss_buc_independent_t(), ss_buc_welch_t()
Between-subjects ANOVA and ANCOVA ss_buc_one_way_anova(), ss_buc_factorial_anova(), ss_buc_factorial_anova_general(), ss_buc_ancova()
Within-subjects and split-plot ANOVA ss_buc_rm_anova(), ss_buc_rm_anova_general(), ss_buc_mixed_anova(), ss_buc_mixed_anova_general()
Correlation and multiple regression ss_buc_correlation(), ss_buc_reg_coef(), ss_buc_R2(), ss_buc_reg_joint()
Multivariate and latent variable ss_buc_manova(), ss_buc_chisq_diff()

The new ones are the one-sample t test, the analysis of covariance, the Pearson correlation (using the exact distribution of its test statistic when both variables are sampled), the two-group multivariate comparison (Hotelling’s T squared), the chi square difference between nested models, and the Welch t test. The Welch planner is an approximation, and a minimum planned sample size of 10 per group is imposed because of estimation accuracy issues at smaller sample sizes, where the approximation is not accurate enough. vignette("worked-examples", package = "BUCSS") walks through one example of each design. Two new vignettes take up particular uses: vignette("planning-replications", package = "BUCSS") shows why a literature of underpowered studies inflates effect sizes and how the correction repairs the plan for a replication, and vignette("correlation", package = "BUCSS") explains when a correlation and a regression slope call for different planners.

Sampled Predictors, Sphericity, and the Planning Effect Size

  • The three regression planners take a random_predictors argument. The default, FALSE, treats the predictors as fixed by design, as in an experiment and as in 1.2.1; TRUE treats them as sampled along with the outcome, as is typical of observational research in the behavioral sciences (Kelley & Maxwell, 2003). Whether the predictors are fixed or sampled changes the distribution of the test statistic, and so the power, when the effect is not zero (Sampson, 1974; Gatsonis & Sampson, 1989). With sampled predictors the planners use the exact distribution of the statistic when the predictors are multivariate normal, for both the correction and the planned study’s power. With one predictor they return exactly what the correlation planner, ss_buc_correlation(), returns.
  • The within-subjects and split-plot planners take an epsilon argument, a Greenhouse-Geisser or Huynh-Feldt sphericity correction, so a prior study reported with corrected degrees of freedom can be planned from. The default, 1, assumes sphericity. Like the Welch planner, the correction is documented as an approximation, with its accuracy in simulation.
  • Every plan reports its planning effect size, an adjusted effect size: the value, in the design’s usual effect size metric, used to plan the sample size given the situation at hand (the prior study’s result, the publication bias assumed through alpha_prior, and the uncertainty allowed for through assurance). It is the adjusted noncentrality parameter restated in units readers know, and it is what the plan is built on, not an estimate of the effect to report: above an assurance of .5 it is deliberately conservative (a lower confidence limit), and at .5 it is the median unbiased estimate. The row is named for its metric: smd_planning, dz_planning (Cohen’s d_z, the mean of the paired differences divided by their standard deviation; the z names the difference score, which Cohen, 1988, writes Z = X - Y), std_mean_planning, f_planning (Cohen’s f), f2_planning (Cohen’s f squared), R2_planning, rho_planning, D2_planning (the squared Mahalanobis distance), or rmsea_d_planning (RMSEA_D, with D for difference: the root mean square error of approximation of the chi square difference test between two nested models, as distinct from the RMSEA of either model’s fit; Savalei, Brace, & Fouladi, 2024).

More Accurate Numbers

The bias and uncertainty adjusted noncentrality parameter is found by root finding rather than a fixed grid, so it is exact and no longer capped at 100 (1.2.1 silently returned a wrong answer above the cap). Some planned sample sizes shift, most by a few units, and each new value is the smallest sample size that actually reaches the target power. df_denominator in ss_buc_factorial_anova_general(), which 1.2.1 ignored, now works. The independent t planner rounds the harmonic mean of two prior group sizes in integer arithmetic, so a pair whose harmonic mean is a whole number no longer plans from a spurious rounding one unit off. An alpha_prior of 1 is computed as exactly 1, where 1.2.1 computed with .999 in its place; most such plans are unchanged and the rest are slightly smaller. A negative observed t is planned from its magnitude, and endpoint or malformed inputs stop with an explanation rather than returning a meaningless number, as does a desired_power at or below alpha_planned, which is not allowable (1.2.1 returned the smallest sample size it considers). Asked for the Factor B effect without levels.B, 1.2.1’s ss.power.ba() and ss.power.wa() silently returned the Factor A plan; in 2.0.0 both stop and ask for the second factor’s levels. Several 1.2.1 functions also fail on current R when effect is omitted; 2.0.0 fixes them.

Clearer Refusals

When the correction cannot be made at the requested assurance, the error reports the largest assurance the prior result can support, which is also printed beneath every result; when a prior result is significant at its own degrees of freedom but not at the balanced design a planner reads it as, the error says so and names an alpha_prior at which a plan can be made. The two refusals carry the condition classes bucss_zero_ncp and bucss_nonsignificant, so code that loops over plans can catch them and nothing else. tidy(), glance(), and planning_sentence() stop with an explanation rather than report one plan’s numbers for another when given several plans stacked into one object or a plan with one of its rows removed, and renaming a plan’s columns returns an ordinary data frame.

Assurance, Explained

The help pages and vignette("understanding-assurance", package = "BUCSS") now spell out how assurance is used, as described above, and show that safeguard power (Perugini, Gallucci, & Costantini, 2014) is a special case. Safeguard power guards against a prior effect size that is too large by planning for the lower limit of a two-sided 60% confidence interval around it rather than for the effect size itself; it allows for uncertainty but not for publication bias. It is BUCSS with alpha_prior = 1 and assurance = .80, that is, without the publication bias correction: with no publication filter, the adjusted parameter is the lower limit of a two-sided 60% confidence interval, and in general a two-sided confidence level C corresponds to an assurance of (1 + C)/2. For F and chi square statistics the two agree exactly. The package help page explains where they differ; every difference makes the plan here the same as the safeguard plan or larger (for the regression planners, within the predictor frame random_predictors names).

Seeing and Auditing a Plan

Calling plot() on a plan draws its assurance ceiling: the largest assurance the prior result can support, the adjusted noncentrality parameter falling to zero there, and the sample size growing asymptotically as it does. Assurance does not degrade gracefully as it rises, it hits a wall, and that is easier to see than to read about.

A plan can also be audited by simulation. ss_buc_sensitivity() takes the result of any planner, simulates prior studies of that design from a true effect you name, discards the ones a literature would not have published, runs the same planner on each survivor, and reports how often a plan built this way actually reaches the target power.

Verified by Simulation

The planners are verified against simulation, and the verification ships with the package so you can rerun it yourself. The harness simulates published prior studies from known true effects and confirms, among other checks, that the corrected noncentrality parameter falls at or below the truth at the requested assurance rate, within simulation error, across every sampling family the package uses; it also checks the correlation planner, the Welch planner, and the regression coefficient planner with sampled predictors against raw simulated data rather than statistics. From any R session with BUCSS installed:

source(system.file("tools", "verify_by_simulation.R", package = "BUCSS"))

The quick mode runs 24 checks in a few seconds; set Sys.setenv(BUCSS_VERIFY = "full") first for published-precision replications, which take under a minute. To audit a specific plan of your own rather than the package at large, use ss_buc_sensitivity(), which runs the same kind of simulation on the design and inputs of any plan you pass it.

Citing BUCSS

If you use BUCSS, please cite the package, which credits the software, its authors, and the version you used:

Kelley, K., Anderson, S. F., & Maxwell, S. E. (2026). BUCSS: Bias and Uncertainty Corrected Sample Size (R package version 2.0.0). https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=BUCSS

For the full set of references, including the methodological articles the correction relies on, run citation("BUCSS") in R.

References

Anderson, S. F., Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2017). Sample-size planning for more accurate statistical power: A method adjusting sample effect sizes for publication bias and uncertainty. Psychological Science, 28, 1547–1562. doi:10.1177/0956797617723724

Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.

Gatsonis, C., & Sampson, A. R. (1989). Multiple correlation: Exact power and sample size calculations. Psychological Bulletin, 106, 516–524. doi:10.1037/0033-2909.106.3.516

Kelley, K., & Maxwell, S. E. (2003). Sample size for multiple regression: Obtaining regression coefficients that are accurate, not simply significant. Psychological Methods, 8, 305–321. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.8.3.305

Perugini, M., Gallucci, M., & Costantini, G. (2014). Safeguard power as a protection against imprecise power estimates. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 9, 319–332. doi:10.1177/1745691614528519
